questions.stem: A 58-year-old male patient presents with difficulty in urination and reports a sensation of incomplete bladder emptying. Upon examination, the neurologist suspects an issue with autonomic innervation to the urinary bladder. What are the root values for the sympathetic and parasympathetic innervation of the urinary bladder?
questions.solutionHtml:
">sympathetic and parasympathetic fibers, involving both motor and sensory functions.
  • Sympathetic innervation controls bladder filling, whereas the parasympathetic innervation controls bladder emptying.
  • Somatic innervation is responsible for the voluntary control of urination.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old woman presents with faecal incontinence, particularly during activities that increase intra-abdominal pressure, such as coughing or lifting heavy objects. MRI reveals atrophy in a muscle responsible for maintaining the anorectal angle. What’s the likely muscle involved in this?
questions.solutionHtml:
27c1692777198f4895cc7c0">sling around the anorectal junction and is crucial for maintaining the anorectal angle.
  • Dysfunction or atrophy of this muscle can lead to faecal incontinence, especially during increases in intra-abdominal pressure.

    • Resting Tone is mainly provided by Internal Anal Sphincter (IAS)

    Relaxed External anal sphincter (EAS) and Puborectalis muscle

    Weakness of External anal Sphincter, Internal anal Sphincter, Puborectalis muscle.

     

    Anorectal Ring Muscles

    Muscle

    Description

    Function

    Significance

    Internal Anal Sphincter (Option D)

    Thickened, terminal portion of the inner circular smooth muscle layer of the large intestine.

    Provides continuous resting tone to the anal canal through sympathetic innervation.

    Dysfunction can lead to faecal incontinence.

    External Anal Sphincter (Option A)

    Main bulk of the anal sphincter complex and is primarily made of striated muscle.

    Allows voluntary control over defecation; allows sustained contraction.

    Important for voluntary faecal control

    Conjoint Longitudinal Muscle (Option B)

    Layer between internal and external anal sphincters; continuous with the outer longitudinal smooth muscle of the rectum.

    Contracts during defecation, shortening and widening the anal canal, facilitating faecal passage.

    Plays a role in defecation; age-related decline in muscle fibres can impact function.

    Puborectalis (Option C)

    Sling muscle part of the levator ani muscle, surrounding the anorectal junction.

    Maintains the anorectal angle.

    Critical for faecal continence

questions.stem: A 46-year-old female reports intermittent rectal bleeding and a feeling of fullness during bowel movements. She has a history of constipation and obesity. Examination reveals internal haemorrhoids. Which of the following options correctly describes their characteristics concerning location and nerve supply? Presence of a visible thrombus in the anal region Ability to manually reduce the mass. Located below the dentate line, covered by anoderm. Innervated by pelvic splanchnic nerves; generally painless.
questions.solutionHtml:
a35341db81">variceal enlargement of the submucosal anal and perianal venous plexuses.
  • They are divided into internal and external piles.
  • Internal Hemorrhoids or True piles are usually painless and occur above the dentate line which bleed on straining during defecation.

    • Type of piles

    Internal Hemorrhoids

    External Hemorrhoids

    Location

    Above pectinate line

    Below pectinate line

    Contributing Vein

    Main tributaries and radicals of Superior rectal vein

    Tributaries of Inferior rectal vein

    Common Site

    3, 7 and 11 o’clock positions of the anal wall, in the lithotomy position

    No such common site.

    Pain

    Painless (as innervated by splanchnic nerves) (Statement 4)

    Painful (innervated by somatic nerves)

    Bleeding

    Bleeds on straining at stool

    Do not bleed on straining

    Points to know
    • Initially, they are contained within the anal canal (1st degree), later, they expand and protrude during defecation (2nd degree), and finally, they stay protruded (3rd degree).
    • 2nd-degree piles can be manually reduced if they are prolapsed and not thrombosed. (Statement 2)
    • A thrombosed external haemorrhoid appears as a painful, swollen, bluish lump at the anal verge resulting from the rupture of a subcutaneous vein. (Statement 1)
    • These are located below the dentate line and present as tense hematomas at the anal margin (perianal hematomas). (Statement 3)

questions.stem: A 33-year-old woman in labour is experiencing discomfort and perianal pain and is scheduled to receive a pudendal nerve block. Which anatomical landmarks should the clinician identify to locate the pudendal nerve accurately?
questions.solutionHtml:
/p>

Explanation:

  • In the pudendal nerve block, the nerve is infiltrated with a local anaesthetic at the point where it crosses the ischial spine using a needle inserted through the vaginal wall, directed by a finger.
  • It aids in achieving almost painless vaginal or forceps deliveries and is also helpful for minor surgeries involving the vagina and perineum.
  • When a bilateral pudendal block is administered, it results in a loss of the anal reflex (saddle anaesthesia), relaxation of the pelvic floor muscles, and diminished sensation in the vulva and lower third of the vagina.

 

Fig: Ischial spine landmark

Fig: Pudendal nerve block

 

Lesser sciatic notch (Option A) is the area where the pudendal nerve exits the gluteal region and enters the pudendal canal. It's not easily accessible for the nerve block.

 

Pubic symphysis (Option B): Administering the block here would not accurately target the pudendal nerve and is unlikely to deliver the intended analgesic effect for perineal pain.

 

Greater sciatic notch (Option C) is the point from which the pudendal nerve enters the gluteal region; it is not the preferred site for nerve block.





1. B. D. Chaurasia’s Human Anatomy, Volume-2, 8th Edition, Page 424, 520 2. Vishram Singh Textbook of Anatomy, Volume-2, 2nd Edition, Page 235

questions.topic: PrepLadder · 38.Neurovascular Anatomy of Pelvis, Perineum, Rectum, and Anal Canal
questions.stem: A 45-year-old woman presents with chronic perineal pain and numbness following a difficult vaginal delivery. The clinician suspects entrapment of the nerve supplying sensation to the perineum. Through which foramina does this nerve exit and re-enter the pelvis?

options.label: B
options.text: Lesser sciatic foramen → Greater sciatic foramen

options.label: D
options.text: Greater sciatic foramen → Lesser sciatic foramen

questions.answerText: Greater sciatic foramen → Lesser sciatic foramen
questions.solutionHtml:
p>

Explanation:

  • Pudendal nerve originates in the pelvis from the anterior rami of the S2, S3 and S4 nerves of the sacral plexus.
  • It enters the gluteal region through the greater sciatic notch, curves behind the ischial spine for a brief distance, and exits the gluteal area by passing into the lesser sciatic foramen.

    Greater sciatic foramen → Obturator foramen (Option A):     Obturator foramen is related to the obturator nerve, not the pudendal nerve.
    Lesser sciatic foramen → Greater sciatic foramen (Option B): This reverses the actual order. The nerve first exits via the greater sciatic foramen and re-enters through the lesser, not the other way around.
    Obturator foramen → Lesser sciatic foramen (Option C): The pudendal nerve doesn't use the obturator foramen. The obturator nerve supplies the medial thigh, not the perineum.





1. Vishram Singh Textbook of Anatomy, Volume-2, 2nd Edition, Page 235 2. B. D. Chaurasia’s Human Anatomy, Volume-2, 8th Edition, Page 424

questions.stem: A 62-year-old female presents with persistent pelvic pain and urinary incontinence. Imaging reveals a mass in the pelvic region compressing nearby blood vessels, raising suspicion of internal iliac artery involvement. Which of the following is not a branch of the internal iliac artery?
questions.solutionHtml:
ta-dictid="837bfc230c16927771892ece07f94b">iliac artery originates from the external iliac artery, not the internal iliac artery.

 

  • Lateral sacral artery (Option A) is a branch of the posterior division of the internal iliac artery, supplying the sacral region.
  • Uterine artery (Option B) branches from the anterior division of the internal iliac artery and supplies the uterus.
  • Internal pudendal artery (Option C) also arises from the anterior division of the internal iliac artery, it supplies the perineum and external genitalia.

  • Common iliac artery is formed by the bifurcation of the abdominal aorta at the L4 vertebra and divides into the external and internal iliac arteries.
  • External iliac artery, after giving off its branches, continues as the femoral artery, while the internal iliac artery splits into anterior and posterior divisions.

questions.topic: PrepLadder · 38.Neurovascular Anatomy of Pelvis, Perineum, Rectum, and Anal Canal
questions.stem: A 50-year-old male presents with painful anal swelling and bleeding. External haemorrhoids are diagnosed, and the physician explains the pain is due to somatic innervation below a specific anatomical landmark in the anal canal. Which of the following separates the areas of somatic and visceral nerve supply in the anal canal?
questions.solutionHtml:
dictid="371930068716927771839cba840631">canal is divided into upper and lower parts by pectinate line or dentate line (teeth shaped), which forms embryological, neurovascular and histological boundaries.
  • Upper part is supplied by the autonomic nervous system (painless) and the lower by somatic nerves (painful).
  • Lower ends of the anal column are joined by short transverse folds of mucous membranes known as anal valves.
  • Mucosal depressions above these valves are called anal sinuses.
  • Together, the anal valves form a transverse line encircling the anal canal, known as the pectinate line.

    • Features

    Upper Anal Canal

    Lower Anal Canal

    Development

    Endodermal

    Ectodermal

    Epithelium

    Simple columnar

    Stratified squamous

    Nerve supply

    Autonomic nerves

    • Painless
    • Sympathetic (L1, L2)
    • Parasympathetic (S2, S3, S4)

    Somatic nerves

    • Painful
    • Sympathetic (S2, S, S4)

    Arterial supply

    Superior rectal artery

    Inferior rectal artery

    Venous drainage

    Superior rectal vein draining into the portal system

    Inferior rectal vein draining into caval system

    Lymphatic system

    Internal iliac nodes

    Superficial inguinal nodes

    Common Type of Hemorrhoids

    Internal hemorrhoids

    External hemorrhoids

    White line of Hilton (Option A) is located at the junction between the subcutaneous portion of the external anal sphincter and the lower border of the internal anal sphincter. It marks the boundary of the mucocutaneous junction.


     

    Anorectal junction (Option B) is defined by the forward convexity of the rectal perineal flexure, located just below the tip of the coccyx. Here, the rectal ampulla narrows as it passes through the pelvic diaphragm, aligning with the apex of the prostate in males.


     

    Iliopectineal line (Option C) is a ridge located on the inner surface of the pelvis, created by the fusion of the ilium and pubis, extending from the pubic symphysis to the arcuate line of the ilium. This anatomical landmark is significant in clinical practice for directing pelvic surgeries and evaluating conditions that impact the pelvic organs.





    1. Vishram Singh Textbook of Anatomy, Volume-2, 2nd Edition, Page 286, 287 2. B. D. Chaurasia’s Human Anatomy, Volume-2, 8th Edition, Page 481,483,484

questions.solutionHtml:
g>‘X’ marked region is the lower part of the rectum. Internal iliac lymph nodes are primarily involved in the lymphatic drainage of the lower part of the rectum.

Lymphatic drainage of anal canal" data-author="NA" data-hash="7679" data-license="NA" data-source="NA" data-tags="April2025" height="500" src="images/q4TLKhg3WfXJ9WXFVQtX1743852721.png"" width="500" />

Para-aortic lymph nodes (Option A) are situated along the abdominal aorta, mainly at the L1 and L2 vertebral levels.
